issues.legal_issue: A court cannot accept selected portions of a witness’s testimony when the witness is unreliable and truth and falsehood are so intermingled that they cannot be separated.
material_facts: The prosecution case depended on one witness after the other eyewitness’s testimony had been wholly rejected.

The remaining witness had been disbelieved in important respects, was found not truthful, and had given a distorted account from the outset, including suppressing the part played by people on his own side.
The High Court accepted some testimony because it accorded with information the witness had earlier given, although it also found that the earlier account was incomplete and distorted.
issues.conclusion: The remaining witness’s testimony had to be rejected in its entirety, and the prosecution case was left unsubstantiated.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the accepted principle that a court may separate truth from falsehood, but must reject the evidence in its entirety when they are so intermingled that separation is impossible. It found it unnecessary to decide whether the evidence of the person who received the earlier account fell within Section 157 of the Evidence Act. No earlier case was cited for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and sole_material_witness_unreliable and account_distorted_from_outset and truth_and_falsehood_inseparable

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.sole_material_witness_unreliable: The prosecution case depends materially on a witness whom the court finds unreliable.
predicates.account_distorted_from_outset: The witness gives a distorted account from the beginning, including suppressing material events or participants.
predicates.truth_and_falsehood_inseparable: The truthful and false parts of the testimony cannot reliably be separated.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction appeal depends on an unreliable witness whose account is distorted from the outset and cannot be separated into reliable and unreliable parts, the testimony is rejected in its entirety.

issues.legal_issue: In a free fight, a person may be held guilty for an injury only when reliable evidence proves that the person caused it.
material_facts: The High Court found that a melee or free fight had occurred, with injuries on both sides.
The court could not reliably determine how the incident began or who inflicted particular blows.
One eyewitness was wholly disbelieved, and the other gave an unreliable account of the participants’ conduct and the infliction of injuries.
issues.conclusion: The convictions could not stand without reliable proof identifying the persons who caused the injuries.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, once the incident was found to be a free fight, only persons proved to have caused injuries could be held guilty for those injuries. The judgment does not rely on an earlier case for this rule.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.free_fight_occurred: The participants on opposing sides engage in a melee or free fight.
predicates.injury_attribution_unreliable: The evidence does not reliably establish who inflicted the particular injuries.

issues.definition: If a criminal conviction appeal concerns a free fight and reliable evidence does not attribute injuries to particular people, the convictions cannot stand without proof of individual injury-causing.

issues.legal_issue: A common intention to commit a criminal act cannot be inferred merely from a shared purpose to assert a claimed right or from the participants’ possession of implements, without reliable proof that they acted in concert.
material_facts: The participants’ asserted purpose was to enforce a claimed right to pass over land.
The inference that some participants intended to use violence rested on one person carrying a spade and others carrying sticks.
There was no proof that those participants had met beforehand, and the Court found no reliable basis for concluding that they acted in concert.
The evidence used to establish their weapons and conduct depended substantially on a witness the Court considered wholly unreliable.
issues.conclusion: The finding of a common intention to force passage by violence was unsupported by the evidence and could not sustain the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, common intention requires proof that the participants acted in concert in furtherance of a common intention to commit a criminal act. A shared intention to enforce a claimed right of way is not itself a common intention to commit a criminal act, and possession of implements alone does not safely establish such an intention. The Court also distinguished Section 34 from Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.shared_purpose_is_only_to_assert_a_claim: The participants share only the purpose of asserting what they believe to be a right.
predicates.implements_are_the_basis_for_inferring_v: The inference that the participants intended violence rests on their possession of implements.
predicates.concert_is_not_reliably_proved: Reliable evidence does not establish that the participants acted in concert.

issues.definition: When people share only a purpose to assert a claimed right, the inference of violence rests on their implements, and concert is not reliably proved, a common intention to commit a criminal act is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A common intention to force passage, even by force if necessary, does not by itself support a culpable-homicide conviction when there is no finding that the participants intended to cause injury.
material_facts: The High Court’s asserted common intention was to force passage through the land, using force if necessary.
The High Court did not find that the participants intended to cause injury to anyone.
issues.conclusion: Even on the assumed finding of a common intention to force passage, the convictions under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code could not be sustained without a finding that the participants intended to cause injury.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the stated common intention to force passage did not satisfy the basis on which the convictions under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code were imposed when the court had not found an intention to cause injury. It noted the distinction between Sections 34 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier case was cited for this holding.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_section_304_convict: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a conviction for culpable homicide.
predicates.common_intention_is_only_to_force_passag: The common intention found is limited to forcing passage, including by force if necessary.
predicates.no_finding_of_intention_to_injure: The court has not found that the participants intended to cause injury to anyone.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges a culpable-homicide conviction based only on a common intention to force passage and there is no finding of an intention to injure, the conviction cannot stand.
